History History Violence in the Troubles play Violence Violence in the Northern Ireland Troubles, 1968 - 1998 Violence in the Troubles The conflict in Northern Ireland during the late 20th century is known as the Troubles. Over 3,600 people were killed and thousands more injured. During a period of 30 years, many acts of violence were carried out by paramilitaries and the security forces. From street battles to car bombs, the evolution of these methods of violence greatly influenced the tactics and impact of the conflict. By July & August 1971 (the marching season), violence was at an all-time high. “NO-GO” areas emerged for the RUC/British Army – particularly in Belfast & Derry. Faulkner’s response to the increasing violence was to introduce “ Internment ” – the arrest and detention of a person without a trial. “ We have to get men of violence off the streets .” Causes of Internment 1) It had previously worked due IRA border campaign (1956-62) 2) Believed it was essential to ending IRA violence & locating IRA weapons Violence continued to increase in NI between 1970 and 1971. Chichester-Clarke in Stormont demanded a stronger response from the new British Conservative PM, Edward Heath. PM Heath did not want to further alienate the Nationalist community. In March 1971, due to inaction from the British Government, Chichester-Clarke resigned.

NI Government Gov ernment was worried about whether the security forces in NI could cope with the increasing violence and tension. July 1969 – violence breaks out in Belfast & Derry. Belfast – houses were burnt by loyalists, which forced Nationalists to leave their homes. Seven people were killed and 100 were wounded. August 1969 Derry – violence began after the Apprentice Boys parade on 12 August, which commemorates the Siege of Derry in 1689. The violence resulted in rioting and violence which is known as the “Battle of the Bogside”. As a consequence, the Irish Taoiseach, Jack Lynch, moved Irish troops and filed hospitals to Donegal/Derry border. Calm was restored in Derry, but broke out again in Belfast. Belfast – violence erupts in all areas of Belfast – it had become a war zone. Seven people died and hundreds were wounded.
